weeks.title: The Elements Toolkit
weeks.intro: Welcome to our listening unit. This week we meet the six elements of music and learn to describe what we hear in clear, musical language.

lessons.title: Active listening and the elements of music
lessons.intention: I can name the elements of music and use them to describe what I hear.
criteria: I can identify at least three elements in a short excerpt.
I can use the right word for each element.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Everyone can hear music. Listening means hearing it in categories.

body.p: You can love a song for years and still not be able to say one useful thing about how it works. That is not a failure of taste. Hearing and listening are different jobs: hearing happens on its own, and listening is deliberate. It is also a skill, which means it improves quickly once you know what you are actually doing.

body.h: The method, and it is only four moves

ul: **Pick one question.** Not the song, not the vibe. One of the six on this page, and only that one.
**Play the excerpt and answer only that question.** Anything else you notice, let go of. It will still be there on the next play.

**Write what you heard, when it happened, and what it did.** A time and a verb. “At 0:52 the bottom of the sound arrives and the whole track gets heavier” is a note you can use later. “Sounds good” is not.
**Play it again with the next question.** Six questions, six passes. In an examination you get three plays, so you spend them on the questions the marks are actually for.

body.p: **Working rule: one question per playing.** Trying to hear everything at once is how you end up hearing nothing, and it is the single most common reason a listening answer comes out as “it builds up and it sounds really good”. Play a track listening only for texture and you will hear things you missed on fifty previous plays. That is not a trick, only attention pointed at one place instead of six.

Every listening question you will be asked, this term and in every examination after it, names one element and asks about that one. Practise hearing them separately and the question has already told you where to listen.

blocks.label: The six questions
blocks.call: The music changes every lesson. The six questions never do.

body.p: Here they are, each with a test you can run on any track in any style, without knowing anything about it in advance. The tests matter more than the definitions: a definition you can recite is worth very little in a listening room.

body.h: Duration: how does it move through time?

body.p: Tap your foot. What you are tapping is the beat, and how quickly you are tapping is the tempo. Count your taps for fifteen seconds and multiply by four, and you have a number you can defend rather than a guess. Then stop tapping and follow the tune instead: the pattern of long and short notes in the tune is the rhythm, and it almost never lines up with your foot. That mismatch is the point of it.

body.h: Pitch: how high or low, and what does the tune do?

body.p: Two questions in one. Where the sound sits, high or low, is its register: try to sing along and notice whether you are straining upwards or growling downwards. What the tune does over time is its contour, which climbs, falls, arches or stays put. Nobody is asking you to name the notes by ear, only to describe the movement.

body.h: Texture: how many layers, and is anything holding the bottom?

body.p: Try to point at the separate things happening at the same time. One voice alone is thin. A voice with a guitar under it is thicker. A full band with something low holding the bottom is thicker again. The most useful version of this question is also the easiest one to answer: is there anything underneath, or is the bottom of the sound empty?

body.h: Performing media and timbre: what is making the sound, and what is that sound like?

body.p: Performing media is the list of what is playing: which voices, which instruments, how many. Timbre is the quality of the sound itself, and it needs an adjective you could defend to somebody who disagrees with you: bright, warm, breathy, buzzy, hollow, thin, rich. This is the one question on the list nothing can answer for you, which is why it rewards knowing the names of instruments. Start collecting them.

body.h: Dynamics and expression: how loud, and does the loudness change?

body.p: Loud and soft, everything between, and what the performer does to shape a note on top of that: an accent, a swell, a note left hanging. The test is a volume knob in your head. Set it at the loudest moment of the excerpt, then ask where the quietest moment sits against it: most of the way down, or barely below? Be careful here, because a passage can sound smaller without getting any softer, and writing “it gets quieter” when nothing got quieter is the easiest mark on this page to throw away.

body.h: Structure: what is the shape of the whole thing?

body.p: This is the only one of the six you cannot hear in a single second. It exists across time: it is the pattern you notice when you compare what you are hearing now against what you heard a minute ago. What you listen for is boundaries, the places where one section stops and another starts. **Working rule: if two or more of the other elements change at the same moment, that moment is a boundary.** One element changing on its own is usually decoration inside a section rather than the start of a new one.
Six questions. Every piece of music ever written answers all six, including the pieces you would never choose to listen to. That is exactly why they are worth having.

blocks.label: Listen
blocks.brief: Play it once, all the way through, before you read a single cue. Write down anything you notice, in any words you like. That first list is yours and nobody marks it. Then come back to the top and work the seven cues below, one at a time, clicking a time to jump the player to it. The cues work through five of the six questions in turn, and the note under them says which one is missing and why.

cues.text: Start with texture, because the opening makes it easy. Listen for what is underneath the sound. Nothing is: the bottom stays empty for the first twelve seconds or so, so what you are hearing is a thin texture with a hole under it. You have just made a texture judgement in one second, without knowing the name of a single instrument on the track.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “The opening, 0:00 to about 0:12, has nothing in the bottom of the sound”: the sub band sits at 0.001 to 0.007 of total energy for the whole window and bass is modest and jumpy (audio_probe window 0-12 at 1 s).

cues.text: The biggest arrival in the first half of the track, and it is worth working out why it feels that big. Two things happen in the same second: the level jumps by about half again, and the bottom of the sound arrives underneath it, four to six times what it had been. Two elements moving together, which by the working rule above makes this a boundary. Write down what changed. Do not write down what the section is called, because nothing you can hear from here proves that.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “0:52 is the biggest arrival in the first half of the track”: chroma-novelty boundary at 0:52.11 with novelty 0.99, rms 0.318 to 0.502, sub 0.015 to 0.086, bass 0.039 to 0.185 (audio_measure boundary list and level profile; audio_probe delta row at 0:52 reads delta rms +0.184 sub+0.071 bass+0.146).

cues.text: Now duration, and you need your foot for this one. Tap the beat, count fifteen seconds of taps, multiply by four, and write the number down before you read anything else. The same count works back at 0:10 and it works here, which is what it means to say the tempo does not change: the arrival at 0:52 made the track heavier, not faster. Those are different elements and they are easy to confuse.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “Tempo: 95.7 beats a minute”: onset autocorrelation over the whole track gives a beat period of 0.627 s, and the same figure comes back over 0:52 to 1:20 alone, so the tempo does not change (audio_probe whole-track window 0-170 at 60 s step, and window 52-80).

cues.text: Dynamics. From here the track empties out, and this is the only time after the opening that it does. Follow the level down across the next six seconds and try to hold on to how far it falls, because you will need it for the worked answer further down the page.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “There is a collapse from 1:50 to 1:56 and it is the quietest the track gets after the intro”: rms 0.503 at 1:50 to 0.155 at 1:56 (audio_probe window 100-174 at 2 s).

sub.text: The first step down, and it is a step rather than a fade: about three quarters of what it was, arriving all at once.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L1, same entry: sustained level event at 1:52.04, down x0.72 (audio_measure level events).

sub.text: The second step, and the bottom of the sound goes with it. By here the track is under a third as loud as it was six seconds ago, which makes this the quietest it has been since the opening.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L1, same entry: sustained level event at 1:56.05, down x0.57, rms 0.155 against 0.503 at 1:50, and sub falling back to 0.006 (audio_measure level events; audio_probe window 100-174 at 2 s).

cues.text: Pitch, and this is the trap the last question warned you about. Everything sounding across the next five seconds is in the top half of the range, with nothing at all underneath it. It is not quiet: the level here is roughly where it was before. So if you write that it gets quieter here, you have named the wrong element and the mark goes with it. Work out which element it actually is before you open the answers at the bottom of the page.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “From about 2:06 to 2:11 there is no low end at all”: bass 0.054 at 2:06 to 0.006 at 2:08 to 0.003 at 2:09, sub 0.000 to 0.001 across the whole span, while rms holds at 0.35 to 0.43 (audio_probe window 124-136 at 1 s).

sub.text: The emptiest second of the passage. There is effectively nothing in the bottom of the sound at all, and the energy has moved up into the top of the range instead.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L1, same entry: at 2:08 bass reads 0.006 and sub 0.000 to 0.001, while high_mid is 0.259 and high 0.288 (audio_probe window 124-136 at 1 s).

cues.text: The bottom comes back, and the track jumps about forty per cent louder in the same second. Two elements moving at once again, exactly like 0:52. Name both of them in your book before you move on. From here to the end nothing collapses again, so this is the last big move the track makes.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “The bottom returns at 2:12”: rms 0.387 to 0.547, up about 41 per cent, with sub +0.052 and bass +0.070 in the same second, and from here to the end the track holds rms 0.50 to 0.62 with no further collapse (audio_probe window 124-136 at 1 s, delta row at 2:12).

cues.text: Structure last, because it is the one question you can only answer once you have heard the whole thing. Follow the ending from here and time it: the track is still at full level at 2:50 and there is nothing left by 2:52, so it stops rather than fades. Now draw the track as a line, left to right, and mark the four big moves on it: 0:52, 1:50 to 1:56, 2:06, and 2:12. That line is a structure answer, and you drew it without needing the word verse or the word chorus once.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “The track ends at about 2:51, and it stops rather than fades”: rms holds 0.556 to 0.642 from 2:44 through 2:50, then 0.381 at 2:50.5, 0.344 at 2:51.5 and 0.023 at 2:52 (audio_probe window 164-173 at 0.5 s). The half-second window was run on 25 August 2026 specifically to settle this, after the two-second window it replaces read as a gradual fall and a cue was written on that reading.

blocks.note: Notice what these cues never do: not one of them tells you which instruments are playing. Every timestamp on this page was measured off this exact recording, and a measurement can say how loud a moment is and which part of the range is sounding, but it cannot say what is making the sound. That is the one question on the list your ears have to answer on their own, and it gets a lesson of its own later in the unit.

blocks.title: The six elements
blocks.prompt: We fill this in together as we meet each one. Write what you listen for.

blocks.summary: If you were away: what each element asks
items: Duration - **speed and time: how fast it goes, and how the notes are grouped and spaced.** Beat, tempo, metre and rhythm all live under this one.
Pitch - **high and low: where the sound sits in the range, and what the tune does over time.** Register, contour and range live here.
Texture - **how many layers are sounding at once, and how they sit against each other.** Thick or thin, and whether anything is holding the bottom.
Performing media and timbre - **what is making the sound, and what that sound is like.** The voices and instruments, and the words for their colour: bright, warm, breathy, buzzy.
Dynamics and expression - **how loud it is, and how the loudness changes.** Loud, soft, sudden, gradual, plus what a performer does to shape a note.
Structure - **the order of the sections, and the shape of the whole thing.** The only one of the six that needs more than a second of music before you can answer it.

blocks.question: Identify one element of music in this excerpt and describe how it is used.
blocks.lead: This is the shape of almost every short listening question you will meet this term, and it is today's task in the same words. Here is one full answer, on the passage you followed at 1:50.
blocks.model: From 1:50 the dynamics fall away in two steps until, by 1:56, the track is under a third as loud as it was and quieter than it has been since the opening, and that emptiness is what makes the full sound at 2:12 land as an arrival rather than as more of the same.

rungs.text: Name the element and say where it is. _Dynamics, from 1:50._ “The dynamics change” names an element but no change and no place, and earns nothing at all.

Say what it sounds like and how far it goes. _Falling away in two steps to under a third as loud, quieter than anything since the opening._ A marker should be able to hear it from your words without playing the track.
Say what it does to the music. _That emptiness makes the return at 2:12 land as an arrival._ This is what the second mark is for, and it is the half most people leave off.

zero.answer: “The dynamics in this song are really effective and add a lot to the mood.”
zero.why: A whole sentence of nothing. It names an element and then says the element is good, which is true of every piece of music ever recorded and therefore says nothing about this one. No time, no sound, no effect. A short answer is fine here. An empty one is not.

blocks.text: Name three elements you heard today.

blocks.summary: Check yourself: four questions on today
items: You counted the beat at 1:00. What number should you have written down, and does it change? **About 95 beats a minute, and no, it does not change anywhere in the track.** Anything from 92 to 98 means you counted rather than guessed.

Two elements move at the same second at 0:52. Which two? **Dynamics, because the whole thing gets louder, and texture, because a layer arrives underneath that was not there before.** You could argue pitch as well, since what arrives is low, and you would not be wrong. The mark is for hearing that two things moved together, which is what makes the moment a boundary.

From 2:06 the track is not quiet, but something has gone. Which element is that a statement about? **Pitch, or register if you want to be exact: everything sounding is in the top half of the range, with nothing under it.** It is not a dynamics answer, because the level barely moved, and that is the most common wrong answer on this page.

Name three elements you heard today, with one word for how each is used. **Any three of: texture, thin at the start; dynamics, sudden at 0:52; duration, steady the whole way through; pitch, high from 2:06; structure, built around four big moves at 0:52, 1:50, 2:06 and 2:12.** The sixth is performing media and timbre, and nothing on this page measured that one for you, so if you named an instrument you heard it yourself.

lessons.title: Duration and pitch (listen and play)
lessons.intention: I can identify duration and pitch features by ear.
criteria: I can describe the tempo, metre and rhythm of an excerpt.
I can describe a melody’s shape (contour) and range.

blocks.text: How music moves through time: is it fast or slow, are the notes short or long, does it have a steady beat or does it feel off-kilter?
How high or low the notes are, and what the melody does: does it climb, fall, stay put?

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Beat, tempo, metre and rhythm are four different things, and only one of them is your foot.

body.p: These four get mixed up more than any other words in music, and it costs marks, because writing “the rhythm speeds up” when you mean the tempo speeds up tells the marker you cannot hear the difference. You do not separate them by memorising four definitions. You separate them by testing them against each other on a real track.

body.h: Four tests, on any track you like

ul: **Tap your foot.** What you are tapping is the beat. It keeps going underneath whether anyone plays a note on it or not.
**Count how quickly you are tapping.** That is the tempo.
**Notice that some taps feel stronger than others.** Strong, weak, weak. Strong, weak, weak. That grouping is the metre, and it is why some music feels like it is in threes and some in fours.
**Now follow the tune instead of your foot.** The pattern of long and short notes in the tune is the rhythm, and it almost never lines up exactly with your tapping. That mismatch is the point of it.

body.p: **Working rule: tempo and rhythm are independent.** Play the same rhythm twice as fast and it is still the same rhythm, just quicker. If you can change one without touching the other, they are not the same thing, and these are the two students collapse into one most often.

body.h: Pitch: describe the motion, not the notes

body.p: Nobody is asking you to name notes by ear. You are being asked to describe movement. A melody's **contour** is its shape over time, whether it climbs, falls, arches or waves. Its **range** is how far it reaches from its lowest note to its highest, which is a separate question: a melody can have a dramatic shape inside a narrow range, or barely move across a wide one. When it moves a small distance to the next note it has stepped, and when it jumps a long way it has leapt. Shape, distance, and how far the whole thing spans. That is the level of detail a listening answer wants.

lessons.title: Writing about music 1
lessons.intention: I can write a clear sentence about how an element is used.
criteria: My sentence names the element.
It says how the element is used and its effect, with evidence.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Writing about music is not saying what you liked. It is reporting what you heard.

body.p: A listening answer is not an essay. It is one short sentence, built on purpose, and the same four moves build every one.

body.h: The four moves, as four questions

ul: **Which element?** Name it: the word for the element, out of the six from Lesson 1, not “it” and not “the music”.
**What does it do that I can hear?** The sound itself, close enough for a reader who has never played the track to picture it.
**What does that do to the music?** Not what it made you feel: what it does to the sound around it, or to where the song is heading.
**Where did I hear it?** A time, a section, or “the whole way through” when that is true.

body.p: **Working rule: one sentence, one element.** A sentence carrying two elements short-changes one of them, and the marker cannot tell which one you were answering. That is why listening answers are dot points and not a paragraph.

Your Lesson 1 notes are most of a sentence already: swap your word for the element word, keep the time you wrote down, and hedge honestly, because “about 95 beats a minute” is trusted and a decimal you never measured is not.

blocks.label: Read this too
blocks.call: Name it, say what it does, say what that does, say where. Four moves, in that order.

body.h: Finding the effect, when nothing comes to mind

body.p: This is the move people stall on. Substitute instead: imagine the same track with that element used the other way, a tempo drifting about instead of holding steady, and ask what has gone missing. What you just named is the effect. Keep it about this track: anything true of every song ever recorded is not an effect at all.
The frame comes back in Lesson 9, where three of these sentences make a full response. For now, one sentence.

blocks.brief: The track from Lesson 1, on purpose. You know it and you have notes on it, so the writing is the new part today.

blocks.question: Describe how one element of music is used in this excerpt.
blocks.lead: Watch this get built rather than reading it finished. It is assembled a move at a time, on duration. The rungs carry the ALARM names your other subjects use, and they are the same four moves as above in the same order: Identify is _name it_, Describe is _how it is used_, Explain is _effect_, and Evidence is _evidence_.
blocks.model: The tempo stays at about 95 beats a minute and never moves, so the speed does nothing to mark one part of the track off from another and the moments that feel bigger are getting their weight from something other than hurry: count the beat at 0:20 and again at 2:20 and it comes out the same.

rungs.text: Name the element and nothing else yet. _The tempo stays at about 95 beats a minute._ Worth no marks alone, and that is the point: you have started the sentence, not finished it.
Say what it does across the excerpt. _... and never moves._ Three words, and they turn a number into something you followed for the whole track.

Say what that does to the music. _... so the speed does nothing to mark one part of the track off from another._ Nothing new was heard here: the hearing happened in the move before. This move is where the second mark lives.
Point at the music so somebody else could check you. _Count the beat at 0:20 and again at 2:20._ Evidence need not be a timestamp, but it must be something a marker could test.

zero.answer: “The song has a really good beat and the tempo is perfect for it.”
zero.why: It names an element and then compliments it. No number, no place in the track, and “perfect” is a verdict rather than a description. The student heard something, then wrote down how they felt.

columns: What it puts in the sentence

blocks.summary: If you were away: the four moves

lessons.title: Performing media and timbre
lessons.intention: I can identify performing media and describe timbre.
criteria: I can name the instruments or voices I hear.
I can describe their tone colour using musical words.

blocks.text: What's making the sound, and what it actually sounds like: an instrument's ‘personality’.

blocks.label: Naming what you hear
blocks.call: Sort by family first. The name comes after, not before.

body.p: You already know more instrument families than you think you do, and you use them without noticing every time you separate one sound from another inside a wall of noise. The problem is never that you cannot hear a separate sound. It is that you reach straight for a name - guitar, drums, whatever the style usually has - before you have actually listened to how the sound is being made. Sort first, name second, and most of the guessing disappears.

body.h: The sorting questions

ul: Voice or instrument? A voice has words, or at least a vowel shape, even when it is wordless.

If it is an instrument, how is the sound started? Plucked or struck (a sharp attack, then the note decays away on its own), bowed or blown (the player can hold the note as long as they like, or make it swell), or electronic (a sound with no obvious physical cause at all - no breath, no string, no skin).
Does the note ring on after it starts, or stop the instant the player stops? A struck bell rings on its own; a drum does not.
Is there one source, or several doing the same job at once? A section of violins moving together sounds different from one violin alone, even before you know the word ‘section’.

body.p: **Working rule: answer those four questions before you reach for a name.** ‘Plucked, decays fast, one source’ gets you to guitar or harp long before ‘sounds like a guitar’ does, and it also gets you somewhere useful when the actual instrument is one you have never heard of. You do not need the exact name to earn the mark. You need a description precise enough that somebody else could not mistake it for a different family.

body.h: When you genuinely cannot name it

body.p: That happens, and it does not have to cost you anything. ‘A struck metal instrument, not a drum’ is a real, defensible answer even if you never learn the exact word for it. What earns nothing is skipping the sorting altogether and writing down whatever instrument the style usually has.

blocks.label: Describing tone colour
blocks.call: A timbre word has to survive being written down without the music playing.

body.p: ‘It sounds nice’ and ‘it sounds warm’ are both one word longer than nothing, but only one of them is a timbre answer. The difference is what the word is describing. ‘Nice’ describes how the sound makes you feel. ‘Warm’ describes a property of the sound itself, and it would still be true of that recording next week, played to somebody in a completely different mood.

body.h: The test

body.p: Ask whether the word could just as easily describe a surface, a light or a temperature as it describes a sound: bright, dark, warm, cold, thin, rich, harsh, smooth, rough, hollow, buzzy, breathy, reedy, metallic, nasal. All of those pass, because they are borrowed from touch and light on purpose - tone colour is a metaphor, and English's whole timbre vocabulary leans on it. ‘Nice’, ‘cool’, ‘sick’, ‘good’ all fail, because none of them describe anything about the sound. They describe you.
**Working rule: if the word could just as easily describe a jumper or a photograph, it is a timbre word. If it only says how you rate the sound, it is not.**

body.h: Where the words come from

body.p: You do not need to invent a word on the spot. Register gives you a head start: a sound sitting high in the range, with most of its energy well above the middle, tends to earn ‘bright’ or ‘thin’; one sitting low and full tends to earn ‘warm’ or ‘rich’. That is a starting point, not a rule you can apply blind - the same register can sound harsh or smooth depending on how the note is started - but it is a faster way in than guessing from nothing.

blocks.label: Listen: solo sitar
blocks.brief: One performer, one instrument, six and a half minutes, recorded at the Darbar festival. Nothing to hide behind and nowhere for a second sound to come from: the hardest possible test of naming and describing, because there is only ever one thing to listen to.

cues.text: A brief low thump right at the start. That is the recording beginning, not the performance: it is gone within five seconds and never returns. Do not count it as an instrument entering.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘The first second is not part of the performance’: at 0:00 the run reads bass 0.360 and sub 0.274 at rms 0.049, and it is gone by 0:05 (audio_probe window 0-40 at 5 s).

cues.text: From here to the very end, listen for what never arrives: almost nothing sounds below 250 Hz on this recording, about one part in a hundred of everything you hear. The middle of the range carries about four fifths of everything you hear, packed into two adjacent bands. A range that narrow is what one sustained source sounds like on its own; more sources than that usually reach wider than this.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, headline table row A (sub+bass 0.012, low_mid+mid 0.802) and ‘From 0:05 to the end, sub reads 0.000 to 0.005 and bass 0.010 to 0.031... low_mid and mid together hold 0.78 to 0.83 throughout the same span’ (audio_probe window 0-40 at 5 s; audio_measure profile). Softened 25 August 2026: the sheet's prose said 'nothing under 250 Hz' but its own figures are sub 0.000 to 0.005 and bass 0.010 to 0.031, so about a hundredth rather than none. The sheet has been corrected to match.

cues.text: Six and a half minutes in, and the bottom of the range is exactly as empty as it was at 0:05: still down around one part in a hundred. Nothing new has ever stepped in underneath this performance. On a page about naming what is making a sound, the honest answer for the register under 250 Hz here is: almost nothing, the whole way through.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘From 0:05 to the end, sub reads 0.000 to 0.005 and bass 0.010 to 0.031, every frame’ - the span this cue sits inside, corrected 25 August 2026 to match the sheet's own figures rather than its earlier prose (audio_probe window 0-40 at 5 s).

blocks.label: Listen: voice and strings
blocks.brief: A solo voice against a string section, with no trumpet or rhythm section audible anywhere on this recording. You meet this same track again as the worked example further down this page, so listen for the media and timbre now and there is less to do later.

cues.text: The first step: loudness jumps by about three fifths in a single second, as the first sound source arrives.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘Only 8 chroma boundaries and 3 sustained level events in 2:18, all three of them in the first fifteen seconds (x1.61 at 0:02...)’ (audio_measure level events).

cues.text: A second step, about half again as loud as the moment before. Something else has just joined what was already sounding.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘...x1.53 at 0:06...’ (audio_measure level events).

cues.text: A third step, and after this one nothing else arrives or drops out for the rest of the track. Whatever is sounding by here is the whole performing ensemble, for the next two minutes.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘...x1.60 at 0:14.2... rms then holds 0.37 to 0.45 for the body of the track... Nothing steps in or out after 0:15’ (audio_measure level events and profile).

cues.text: Across the body of the track, the middle of the range carries about three fifths of the sound's energy between two adjacent bands, with about a quarter reaching above 2500 Hz. A texture that sits in the middle rather than reaching for brightness: match that to what is carrying the tune and what is sitting underneath it.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘Band spread across the body: low_mid 0.305 and mid 0.305 with high_mid 0.131 and high 0.109’ (audio_measure profile). Corrected 25 August 2026: the sheet's figure is 0.240, which is about a quarter rather than around a fifth.

cues.text: The single biggest harmonic change on the whole track happens here, and it is quieter than the body around it, not louder: a change carried by less of the sound than usual. With the ensemble pulled back like this, one of the two sources you have been listening for should be more exposed than the other. Listen for which one is carrying that change alone.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘The highest chroma novelty on the track is at 2:03.1 (novelty 1.00), at rms 0.206, which is lower than the body of the track’ (audio_measure boundary list).

blocks.label: Listen: full orchestra
blocks.brief: The recording's own title is only “Main Title”, with no film name or year on record; the channel credited is John Williams. Nearly five and a half minutes, built around two huge arrivals rather than one - the opposite shape to the voice and the sitar you have just heard.

cues.text: Before the first big arrival, this track is nearly silent: barely above a whisper, and almost all of what little is sounding sits in the middle of the range.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘At 1:28 and 1:30 rms reads 0.044, against 0.35 for the body of the piece, with mid alone carrying 0.48 of what little there is’ (audio_probe window 88-100 at 2 s).

sub.text: The arrival begins: loudness starts climbing out of that near-silence.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘rms goes 0.044 at 1:30 to 0.150 at 1:32’ (audio_probe window 88-100 at 2 s).

sub.text: The bottom of the range arrives with it: a band that was barely present a moment ago now carries about eight times what it did, in the same stretch the loudness keeps climbing.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘bass comes up with it from 0.021 at 1:30 to 0.173 at 1:36’ and ‘rms... 0.498 at 1:36’ (audio_probe window 88-100 at 2 s; audio_measure level events).

sub.text: By here the arrival is complete: loudness has multiplied more than eleven times across the whole ten seconds from 1:28, which is the biggest arrival anywhere in this recording. Two different things are being measured when you compare arrivals: how far the level travels across the whole arrival, and how big its single largest step is. This one doubles in its largest step, like the two that follow, and the eleven times is the whole journey out of near-silence. A change this large, spread across this much of the range, is the shape a full ensemble makes when it comes in together, not one instrument.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘rms goes 0.044 at 1:30 to... 0.518 at 1:40, which is more than eleven times over ten seconds... A sustained level event marks it at 1:34.3, up x2.01’ (audio_probe window 88-100 at 2 s; audio_measure level events).

cues.text: A second arrival, and it is about the same size as the first: the level roughly doubles again in one step, just as it did at 1:34. The same kind of jump as before, not just a louder moment - when a change this size repeats, it usually means the same forces coming back rather than new ones arriving.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘A second one of the same size at 3:11.6, up x2.06’, read against the first arrival's own ‘1:34.3, up x2.01’ (audio_measure level events). Rewritten 25 August 2026: the first version printed the raw multipliers 'x2.06' and 'x2.01', which are the only raw figures anywhere on this site's student pages and have no key, and it cross-referenced 1:34, which carries no cue.

cues.text: A third arrival, but a smaller one this time: up by about two fifths, against the doubling of the first two. A jump this size is consistent with fewer performing forces returning, or the same ones re-entering more quietly, rather than an arrival on the scale of 1:40 or 3:12. Listen for whether this sounds like the same forces as before or something smaller.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘a smaller one at 4:36.8, up x1.41’, read against the two earlier arrivals at x2.01 and x2.06 (audio_measure level events).

cues.text: Now the bottom disappears again while the top does not: almost nothing below 250 Hz, while the middle and upper-middle of the range are still sounding clearly. Whatever is carrying the tune up there has been left on its own.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘At 4:55 the bottom is gone and the top is not: bass 0.005 and sub 0.002 while mid reads 0.421 and high_mid 0.302, at rms 0.214’ (audio_measure profile).

cues.text: The ending is a fall in two steps, not a fade: down to about a third of what it was, then down again to a little over a third of that, in the space of four seconds. That is a texture cut in blocks, the kind of ending you get from an ensemble stopping together, not one instrument trailing off on its own.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L5, ‘sustained events at 5:13.4 down x0.35, 5:17.4 down x0.37’ (audio_measure level events).

blocks.note: Set the three side by side, because this is the one thing on this page you can count rather than guess. The sitar puts about four fifths of its energy into two neighbouring middle bands, with about one part in a hundred below 250 Hz. Armstrong spreads wider: about three fifths through the middle, about a seventh below 250 Hz and about a quarter above 2500 Hz. The orchestra spreads widest of the three, a little over half through the middle. That spread is not a coincidence of the recording. It is what more sound sources playing at once does to the range, and it is why the three sound as far apart as they do before you have named a single instrument.

blocks.title: Performing media words
blocks.prompt: We fill these in together. Write what each one means.

blocks.title: Instrument families
blocks.prompt: Different job: name one instrument you heard from each family.

blocks.summary: If you were away: performing media words
items: **Solo** - one performer, alone.
**Duet** - two performers.
**Trio** - three performers.
**Quartet** - four performers.
**Ensemble** - any group playing or singing together; the general word when nothing more specific fits.
**Orchestra** - a large mixed ensemble built from string, woodwind, brass and percussion sections together.
**Choir** - a group of singers, usually more than one voice on each part.
**A cappella** - voices alone, with no instruments at all.
**Rhythm section** - the instruments holding the beat and the harmony underneath everything else: usually some mix of drums, bass, guitar and keyboard.

blocks.summary: If you were away: instrument families
items: **Strings** - any instrument that makes its sound from a vibrating string, plucked, bowed or struck: violin, cello, guitar, sitar, harp.
**Woodwind** - a column of air set vibrating by breath across or through a reed or an edge: flute, clarinet, oboe, saxophone.
**Brass** - a column of air set vibrating by the player's own lips against a mouthpiece: trumpet, trombone, French horn, tuba.
**Percussion** - struck, shaken or scraped: drum kit, timpani, tambourine, cymbals.
**Keyboard** - played with keys, however the sound is actually produced underneath them: piano, organ, synthesiser.
**Electronic** - a sound with no obvious physical cause: synthesiser, drum machine, an electric instrument run through an effect.
**Voice** - the human voice itself, described by range or style rather than an instrument name: soprano, tenor, gravelly, spoken.

None of today's three recordings has a keyboard or an electronic instrument in it: the sitar excerpt is one string instrument alone, the Armstrong excerpt is voice and strings only, and the orchestra draws on strings, woodwind, brass and percussion, which is what ‘full orchestra’ means. Those two rows are legitimately blank today, not something you missed.

This table has no single fixed answer, because it asks what you heard, not what is always true. The right answer is the real instrument you can point to in one of today's three recordings and defend if somebody disagrees with you.

Work through the three guided listens, one per excerpt, using the register cues to help place what you hear.
Fill in the performing media and instrument family tables on this page as we go.
Build a class timbre word bank from what you hear, checked against the test above.
Read the worked example, then write your own on one of the other two excerpts.

blocks.question: Identify the performing media in this excerpt and describe its timbre.
blocks.marks: 2 marks - one for performing media, one for timbre
blocks.lead: This is the shape of the actual exam question: performing media and timbre are worth two marks together, one for naming what you hear and one for describing it. Here is one full answer, on the Armstrong recording above.
blocks.model: This is a solo voice set against a string section, with no other instrument audible anywhere in the recording: a warm, breathy vocal tone over a smooth, sustained string tone underneath it.

rungs.text: Name what is making the sound, precisely enough that somebody else could recognise the same recording from your words. _A solo voice, with a string section behind it and nothing else audible._ Getting the family right earns the mark, even without naming every player in the section.

Give a real timbre word for what you named, not a vague one. _Warm and breathy for the voice, smooth and sustained for the strings._ Both words would survive being written down without the recording playing, which is the test from earlier on this page.

zero.answer: “It sounds beautiful and really sets the mood.”
zero.why: A taste judgement, not a listening answer. It never says what is making the sound, so the first mark is not there, and ‘beautiful’ is not a tone colour word: it says how the answer-writer feels, not what the recording sounds like, so the second mark is not there either.

blocks.summary: If you were away: the other two excerpts
items: **Sitar excerpt** - performing media: a solo sitar, one instrument playing alone with nothing else audible. Timbre: a buzzy, resonant plucked-string tone with a steady drone underneath it - a sound that almost never reaches down into the bottom of the range, about one part in a hundred of what you hear, which is part of what makes it feel so exposed.

**Orchestra excerpt** - performing media: a full orchestra, strings, woodwind, brass and percussion all contributing rather than one instrument on its own. Timbre: rich and full when the whole ensemble is playing together, thinning to a brighter, less full sound at the moments when only the middle and upper parts of the range are left sounding.

blocks.text: Pick one instrument and describe its timbre in a full sentence.

blocks.summary: Check yourself: four questions on today
items: What is the difference between performing media and timbre? **Performing media is what is making the sound - the voices and instruments. Timbre is what that sound is actually like.**
How much of the sitar recording's sound sits below 250 Hz, from 0:05 to the very end? **Almost nothing - about one part in a hundred of everything you hear, the whole six and a half minutes.**
On the Armstrong recording, when does the ensemble finish arriving? **By about 0:15. Nothing steps in or drops out again for the rest of the track.**

What is the test for whether a timbre word is actually doing its job? **It has to describe the sound the way you would describe a surface or a light: warm, bright, harsh, thin. If it only says how the sound made you feel, it fails the test.**

teacher: Use the ‘Elements of Music’ deck (timbre section).

lessons.title: Comparing “Valerie”
lessons.intention: I can compare two versions of the same song using performing media and timbre.
criteria: I can name the voices and instruments I hear in each version.
I can describe the tone colour of each one using musical words.
I can write one similarity and one difference, and back each up with musical evidence.

blocks.text: The voices and instruments used to perform a piece of music: in other words, what is making the sound.

The quality of a sound that makes one voice or instrument sound different from another, even when they play exactly the same note. A trumpet and a flute playing the same pitch do not sound the same, and timbre is the word for that difference.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Performing media is a list. Timbre is a description. The question always wants both.

body.p: These two elements arrive together in every listening paper you will ever sit, and they ask two different things of you. Performing media is a list of what is making the sound: the voices, the instruments, how many of them. Timbre is what those sounds are actually like. You can get the list completely right and still write nothing worth a mark, because a list is not a description.

body.h: Naming what you can hear, one layer at a time

body.p: Nobody names six things at once on a first play. Take one pass per layer, in this order, and write one line after each pass:

ul: **The lead voice.** One singer, or more than one? Sitting comfortably, or reaching?
**Whatever carries the tune when nobody is singing.** In the gaps, and in any introduction or ending.
**Whatever holds the pulse.** The layer you would tap along with. It is usually low, and usually the last thing people notice, because it is the thing you feel rather than the thing you listen to.
**Whatever fills the middle.** Chords, riffs, sustained sounds: anything sitting between the pulse and the voice.
**Anything that happens once.** A single hit, a stab, a sound that never comes back. These are what separate a good answer from a full one.

body.p: **Working rule: name only what you actually heard.** A guess that is wrong costs you more than a gap does, because the marker now knows you were not listening. _A low sustained instrument holding the bottom_ is an honest answer and it earns something. An instrument that is not in the recording earns less than nothing.

body.h: Describing the colour, so somebody could hear it from your words

body.p: A timbre word is only worth writing if you can say what made you choose it. Run three tests on the sound in front of you, in any order:

ul: **High or low, and how much of the range does it fill?** This is the test that separates rich from thin, and full from hollow.
**Smooth or rough?** Is there grit, buzz or rasp on the surface of the sound, or is it clean? This separates mellow from harsh, and polished from raw.

**How does a note start?** Struck and gone, or eased in and held? A sound with a hard edge on the front of every note reads as bright even when it is not especially high, which is the single most common reason people put the wrong word down.

body.p: Then attach the word to its source. **Every timbre word needs a sound source in the same sentence.** _The tone colour is warm_ is worth nothing, because it does not say what is warm. _The lead voice is husky, with a rough edge on the held notes_ is a description a marker can hear without playing the track, and that is the whole job.
Words that describe your reaction rather than the sound cannot be marked: nice, good, cool, catchy, sick, vibey. If a word would fit a sandwich as easily as a saxophone, leave it out.

blocks.label: Comparing two versions
blocks.call: When the tune, the words and the chords are held still, everything you can still hear is a difference in the performing.

body.p: A cover keeps the song and replaces the performance. The melody is the same, the words are the same, the chords are the same. So every difference you can hear between these two recordings is a difference in how they were performed: who is playing, what they are playing, how fast they take it, how it was recorded. That makes a pair of versions the cleanest listening test there is, because the thing you are comparing is the only thing that changed.

body.h: Writing the comparison

body.p: One similarity and one difference, and each one in three parts:

ul: **Name it.** Which element, and which version. _The 2007 version's low register_ is a name. _It sounds different_ is not.
**Give the evidence.** What you heard, and when. A time makes the claim checkable, and a claim nobody can check is worth about half of one that can be.
**Say what it does.** The effect on the person listening. This is the part most people leave off, and it is usually the part carrying the second mark.

body.h: Three traps on this pair, and all three catch people

ul: **The second video does not start with the song.** It opens with about fifty seconds of a film scene. The song itself begins at about 0:51, so every time you write for that version is counted from there. Go looking for the first verse at 0:05 and you will find dialogue.

**The two clocks do not match.** These versions run at different speeds, so the same moment of the song lands at different times on the two videos, and the gap widens as they go. Never compare 1:30 in one with 1:30 in the other. Compare events with events: the first entry of the voice against the first entry of the voice.

**Speed is not tone colour.** The difference in speed is the largest measurable difference between these two recordings and it is well worth writing about, but it belongs to duration. Label it correctly. An answer that offers a tempo difference as a difference in timbre has named the wrong element, and loses the mark it had already earned.

body.p: One last thing, and it is the honest limit of this page. Every timestamp in the two guides below was measured off these exact recordings, and a measurement can say how loud a moment is and which part of the range is carrying the sound. It cannot say what is making the sound, so this page never prints the list of instruments for either version. The naming is yours. What you have instead of a printed list is better than one: both of these are official videos of the performers playing, so once you have written your list from sound alone, you can play the video again, watch it, and check your list against what you can see. Listen first, then look. Look first and you will hear what you expected to see, which is not listening at all.

blocks.label: Version A: the original
blocks.brief: Play it once with nothing to do but notice. Then come back to the top and work the cues, clicking a time to jump the player to it. Your job on this version is the list first, then the colours: the lead voice, whatever holds the pulse, whatever fills the middle, and three tone-colour words you could defend to somebody who disagreed with you.

cues.text: No introduction to speak of. The level steps up here, and by 0:06 the track is at the weight it holds for the next three and a half minutes, so the whole line-up is in front of you inside six seconds. Use them: name the lead voice, then one layer underneath it, before the song has a chance to distract you.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “The Zutons video has no such intro”: a level event at 0:02.00, up x1.42, and by 0:06 the track is at full weight, rms 0.503 (audio_measure level events; audio_probe window 0-30 at 3 s).

cues.text: Now ask where this version puts its weight. Almost all of it is in the upper middle of the range: for practically the whole track the very bottom of the sound carries somewhere between a hundredth and a twentieth of it, while the upper middle carries between a quarter and a third. Register is not the same thing as tone colour, but it tells you where to point your ears, and up there is where this version lives. Name two things you can hear in that upper middle, and give each one a word.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “The other measured contrast: how much bottom each version has”: on the Zutons, sub sits at 0.01 to 0.05 and bass at 0.10 to 0.16 for almost the whole track while high_mid holds 0.26 to 0.35, so “the weight of the sound is in the upper middle” (audio_measure five-second profiles; audio_probe windows 0-30 and 150-190 on A).

cues.text: Count the beat. Tap along, count your taps for fifteen seconds, multiply by four, and write the number in your book. Speed is duration, not timbre, so it is not the element of today's lesson, and it is still worth thirty seconds of your time: the comparison you have to write wants a difference you can back up, and this is the one difference between these two recordings you can measure yourself with a foot and a clock. Do the same on the other version and keep both numbers.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “Zutons: 83.4 beats a minute (beat period 0.720 s, autocorrelation peak 0.496 of lag zero), measured over 0:05 to 3:40” (audio_probe, whole-song window). The figure is kept out of the cue on purpose, so that the counting is real; the check at the foot of the page hands it back.

cues.text: Pick any moment between here and the end, and it is at much the same weight as 0:06 was. Across three and a half minutes the level never leaves a narrow band, the harmony turns a corner only six times in the whole song, and frame to frame the sound changes about half as much as the other version's does. So the line-up you wrote down at the start is very likely still the line-up you are hearing now. Check that by ear, because the measurement cannot check it for you: all it can say is that if anything left, it left quietly.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “Zutons: how little else happens”: only six chroma-novelty boundaries in 3:52, none above novelty 0.42 until the ending, and rms sits between 0.46 and 0.60 from 0:06 to 3:45 apart from the 2:34 dip; and “Ronson: how much more happens”, spectral flux 0.18 to 0.26 on the Zutons against 0.45 to 0.53 on the Ronson (audio_measure boundary lists and profiles on both).

cues.text: The one place in this track where the band gets out of the way, and the best fifteen seconds on the page for hearing a tone colour on its own. Over the next ten seconds the level falls to under a third of what it is right now, the bottom of the sound very nearly disappears, and the top of it climbs. Fewer things sounding means each one is easier to name and easier to describe, so this is where you collect your colour words for this version.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “Zutons: the one place the band gets out of the way”: rms 0.508 at 2:32 to 0.154 at 2:42, under a third, and bass 0.143 at 2:32 to 0.022 at 2:36, while high climbs the other way, 0.097 at 2:32 to 0.291 at 2:42 (audio_measure level events; audio_probe window 150-190 at 2 s).

sub.text: The first step down, and it is a step rather than a fade: about three quarters of what it was, arriving all at once.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L6, same entry: a sustained level event at 2:34.83, down x0.72 (audio_measure level events).

sub.text: Four seconds in and the floor has gone: the low band is down to about a sixth of what it held at 2:32. Whatever was holding the bottom of this track has stopped, which means you can now hear what had been sitting on top of it.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L6, same entry: bass 0.143 at 2:32 to 0.022 at 2:36 (audio_probe window 150-190 at 2 s).

sub.text: The quietest the track gets between its start and its ending: under a third of the level it ran at ten seconds ago. The energy has moved to the top of the range as well, where the highest band has roughly tripled since 2:32. Low sounds gone, high ones left. Two colour words minimum before you move on.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L6, same entry: a sustained level event at 2:41.08 down x0.72, rms 0.154 at 2:42 against 0.508 at 2:32, and high 0.097 at 2:32 to 0.291 at 2:42 and 0.320 at 2:44, with rms otherwise between 0.46 and 0.60 from 0:06 to 3:45 (audio_measure level events; audio_probe window 150-190 at 2 s).

cues.text: And back, about half again as loud in a single step. Now listen to what does not come back with it: the bottom of the sound is still nearly as empty here as it was in the dip, and it does not return to the weight it had before until about 2:54, eight or nine seconds later. The level and the low end come back separately, and hearing that gap is what separates a real answer from a guess. So the shape to remember on this version is out of the way, then back in stages, about twenty seconds from 2:34 to 2:54. The other version does nothing like it.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “Then it comes back: 2:45.09 up x1.46, rms 0.317 at 2:46 to 0.572 at 2:58, bass back to 0.128 to 0.149”, read at the resolution of the claim: in the same run the bass band is still 0.051 at 2:46, 0.020 at 2:50 and 0.080 at 2:52, and only reaches 0.124 at 2:54 and 0.149 at 2:56, against 0.143 at 2:32. So the level returns about eight seconds before the weight underneath does, and the sheet's “bass back to 0.128 to 0.149” describes 2:54 onwards, not 2:46 (audio_measure level events; audio_probe window 150-190 at 2 s).

blocks.note: Not one cue above names an instrument, and that is deliberate. What was measured is level and register, and neither of those can say what is making a sound. Every name in your book is one you put there yourself, and the video above is how you check it: write your list from sound alone, then play it again and watch.

blocks.label: Version B: the cover
blocks.brief: Do not press play and start writing. This video opens with about fifty seconds of a film scene, and **the song does not begin until about 0:51.** Every time you write for this version counts from there. Work the cues in order, then do the same two jobs you did on the original: the list, then the colours.

cues.text: Still not the song. Listen to what this sound is made of: there is effectively nothing in the bottom of the range, somewhere between a five-hundredth and a hundredth of it, and everything is stacked in the middle and upper middle. That is what talking measures like, and it is worth hearing, because it is the exact opposite of what arrives at 0:51. Write nothing down yet.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “The Ronson video does not start with the song. It starts with about fifty seconds of film scene”: 0:00 to about 0:41 has almost no bottom at all, sub 0.002 to 0.009 and bass 0.006 to 0.013 across 0:24 to 0:30, with energy piled in mid and high_mid, “which is what speech reads as” (audio_probe window 0-60 at 3 s).

cues.text: The scene runs out. Across these few seconds what is left falls to under a third of itself and then holds at almost nothing. If you ever lose your place on this video, find this gap: the song is on the other side of it.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “0:42 to 0:50 falls away to near silence: rms 0.237 at 0:42, 0.066 at 0:45 and 0:48” (audio_probe window 0-60 at 3 s).

cues.text: The song. This is the largest single step anywhere in the file, the level up by more than two and a half times in one moment, and the harmony turns over completely at the same instant. Listen to where the new sound sits: about a fifth of everything you can now hear is in the very bottom of the range, where a second ago there was nothing at all. Something low has arrived. Name it if you can hear what it is, describe where it sits if you cannot, and from here on treat 0:51 as this version's zero.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6: “A sustained level event at 0:50.81, up x2.61 - the largest step on the track by a distance - and a chroma boundary at 0:51.59, novelty 0.98”, and “From 0:51 the bottom is suddenly there: sub 0.177 at 0:51 and 0.234 at 0:54, bass 0.19 to 0.25” (audio_measure level events and boundary list; audio_probe window 0-60 at 3 s).

sub.text: Three seconds later there is more down there, not less: nearly a quarter of the whole sound is in the bottom band. This opening stretch has more weight underneath it than anywhere else on either version, so it is the easiest place on the page to hear what separates the two recordings.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “sub 0.234 at 0:54” and “in the first verse after 0:51 sub reaches 0.18 to 0.23”, against the Zutons' sub of 0.01 to 0.05 for almost its whole track (audio_probe windows 0-60 and 110-135 on B, 0-30 and 150-190 on A; audio_measure five-second profiles on both).

cues.text: Count the beat here, exactly as you did on the original. Do it before you look at the number you wrote over there, so that you are not talking yourself into an answer. The two numbers sit further apart than almost anybody guesses, and that gap is the one difference between these recordings you can prove without naming a single instrument.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “Ronson: 107.7 beats a minute (beat period 0.557 s, autocorrelation peak 0.622 of lag zero), measured over 1:00 to 4:00”, against the Zutons' 83.4, which is “the Ronson version running about 29 per cent faster” (audio_probe, whole-song windows on both tracks).

cues.text: Stop naming things for a moment and listen to how fast the surface of this music moves. Frame to frame it changes about twice as much as the original does, and across its length it turns three times as many harmonic corners. That is a measurement of activity, not of how many instruments are playing, so do not write it up as a texture answer. What it means for you is practical: colours arrive and leave faster here, so you need shorter listening windows to catch them than you needed on the original.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “Ronson: how much more happens”: twenty-one chroma-novelty boundaries against the Zutons' six, and spectral flux 0.45 to 0.53 across the whole track against the Zutons' 0.18 to 0.26; “Flux counts how much the sound changes frame to frame, so this is a claim about surface activity, not about how many instruments there are” (audio_measure boundary lists and profiles on both).

cues.text: A step down, to about three quarters, and it holds rather than bouncing straight back. This is the one sustained drop inside the song, and a drop is your best chance at an individual colour, because there is less piled on top of it. Listen twice: once to decide whether anything actually left, and once to decide whether everything simply got quieter. Those are different events, and only your ears can tell them apart.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “Ronson: how much more happens”: a sustained level drop at 2:01.00 down x0.72 inside the song (audio_measure level events).

cues.text: And a step back up, about a quarter louder, held. Those are this version's two big level moves, and they sit a full minute apart. The original does something that looks similar on paper and is not: its drop and its recovery are ten seconds apart. Same pair of moves, entirely different shape. Writing that the two versions handle their quiet moment the same way is the easiest wrong answer available today.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “Ronson: how much more happens”: a rise at 3:02.07 up x1.28 inside the song, set against the Zutons' drops at 2:34.83 and 2:41.08 and its recovery at 2:45.09 (audio_measure level events on both).

cues.text: Full weight here, and about fourteen seconds of song left. Stop your comparison at 4:24: from there the bottom of the sound goes to nothing and the level falls away, and what runs on to the end of the file is not the track. Anything you write about how this version ends has to be about what happens before 4:24.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L6, “It ends early too”: rms holds 0.52 to 0.56 through 4:10 to 4:20, then bass falls to 0.023 at 4:24 and 0.004 at 4:28 and rms to 0.220, with the last twelve seconds at rms 0.066 and below, so “the song is over by about 4:24” and the file runs to 4:40.8 (audio_probe window 250-278 at 2 s).

blocks.note: Every time above is this video's own clock. This version runs faster than the original, so nothing here has a matching timestamp over there, and a comparison written by lining the two clocks up will be wrong on every line. Compare events with events. Same rule as the original for the naming, too: write your list from sound alone first, then watch.

blocks.title: Timbre words worth defending
blocks.prompt: Twelve words from the bank above. Write what each one means, and one sound you would use it about. We fill this in as we go.
columns: What it means, and a sound it fits

blocks.summary: If you were away: the twelve timbre words
items: **Bright** - plenty of energy at the top of the sound, with a hard edge on the front of each note. It cuts through whatever else is playing. A trumpet high in its range, or a cymbal struck hard.

**Dark** - the opposite: the top is missing or covered over, so the sound feels closed in. Not the same as quiet, and not the same as low. A clarinet at the bottom of its range, or a piano played with the soft pedal down.

**Warm** - full in the lower middle, smooth on the surface, no hard edges anywhere. The word most people reach for when a sound is comfortable to sit inside. A cello in its middle register, or an electric piano played gently.
**Mellow** - soft-edged and even, with nothing sticking out of it. A warm sound played gently: a flugelhorn, or a nylon-string guitar picked with the fingers.

**Harsh** - rough and hard at once, with an edge that grates rather than excites. Worth saying when it is deliberate, and it often is. An electric guitar with the distortion up, or a saxophone pushed hard at the top of its range.

**Rich** - a lot going on inside the one note, high and low together, so a single sound seems to fill the range on its own. A pipe organ with several stops pulled out, or a grand piano with the sustain pedal down.
**Thin** - the opposite of rich. A narrow sound with nothing underneath it and not much around it. A recorder, or one voice singing alone.

**Hollow** - the middle of the sound is missing while the outsides are still there. It sounds like something with a hole in it, because usually it is. Blowing across the top of a bottle, or a marimba bar struck softly.
**Husky** - a voice with air and grain in it, slightly rough, a little worn. A word for voices far more often than for instruments, and it fits a singer working near the bottom of their range.
**Breathy** - you can hear the air moving as well as the note. Common in a quiet voice, or a flute low in its range.
**Nasal** - pinched and narrow, as though the sound is coming out through a small opening. It describes a shape, not a fault. An oboe, or a harmonica.

**Raw** - unpolished on purpose: rough edges left in and nothing smoothed off. The word for a recording that sounds like a room rather than a studio, or a voice recorded with nothing done to it afterwards.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Copy both definitions into your book, and the timbre word bank.
Play each version once with nothing to do but notice. Then work the cues underneath it, clicking a time to jump the player.
The second video opens with a film scene: the song itself starts at about 0:51, and your times for that version count from there.
Rule up a table in your book with a column for each version: the lead voice, whatever holds the pulse, whatever fills the middle, anything that happens once, and three tone-colour words.

Name what you can hear with your eyes off the screen, and write it in the table. Then play each video again and watch it, and check your list against what you can see being played. Listen first, look second.
Fill in the timbre words table on this page as we go.
Write your comparison: one similarity and one difference, each in three parts. Name it, give the evidence with a time, say what it does.
Working alone? Everything you need is here: the cues, the two videos to check your naming against, and the answer sections you can open on this page.

blocks.summary: If you were away: how to check your own naming
items: Nobody is here to tell me whether my list is right, so how do I check it? **Listen first and write the list from sound alone. Then play each video again and watch it: both are official videos of the performers playing, so the picture is your marking key. Confirm what you had, correct what you got wrong, and add what you missed.** Do it in that order and no other. Watch first and you will hear what you expect to see, which teaches you nothing.

Why does this page not simply print the list? **Because naming by ear is the skill being learned, and a printed list lets you skip it. Nothing on this page measured what is making the sound, so the only honest marking key for the naming is the recording itself.** The times, the levels and the registers were measured, and they are all handed back to you somewhere on this page. The names were not measured, so they are not.

What the picture will not tell me. **A video shows what is in shot, and that is not always everything you can hear: something can be playing without being on camera, and a studio recording can carry layers nobody filmed.** So if you can hear a layer you cannot see, keep it. Write what you heard, say where it sits in the range and what it sounds like, and note that you could not confirm it. An honest unconfirmed line is worth more than a confident wrong name.

My book table, row by row: what does a full entry look like? **The lead voice: how many singers, and whether they sound like they are reaching or sitting comfortably. Whatever holds the pulse: the layer you would tap along with, and whether it sits low or high. Whatever fills the middle: what is between the pulse and the voice, and whether it is sustained or moving. Anything that happens once: the time it happens and what it sounds like. Three tone-colour words: one each for the voice, the pulse layer and the middle, taken from the bank and written beside the sound it belongs to.** The first four rows are the ones the video can confirm for you. The last row it cannot, because a colour word is a judgement rather than a fact: yours is right if you can say what made you choose it.

blocks.text: Write one similarity and one difference between the two versions, each backed with musical evidence and its effect. Performing media and timbre are marked together as one 2-mark question in the listening exam: naming the instruments alone only gets you one mark, you need the tone-colour description too.

blocks.question: Describe one difference between these two versions of “Valerie”, using musical evidence.
blocks.lead: This is the shape of the comparison you are writing today, and the shape of the comparison question in a listening paper. Here is one full answer, built on something you can hear rather than something you assumed.
blocks.model: The 2007 version carries far more of its sound low in the range than the 2006 one does: from the moment the song starts at 0:51, about a fifth of everything you can hear is in the very bottom of the sound, where the original keeps its weight up in the upper middle for the whole three and a half minutes, so the newer version feels heavy and pushed along from underneath while the original sounds lighter and thinner under the voice.

rungs.text: Name the difference and say which version it belongs to. _The 2007 version has much more low sound in it._ If you can hear what is making that low sound, name the instrument instead, because naming is what performing media is for. Name only what you actually heard: a wrong name costs you more than a gap does. _They sound different_ names nothing and earns nothing.

Give the evidence, and put a time on it. _From 0:51, about a fifth of the sound is right at the bottom of the range, and the original keeps almost nothing down there at any point._ A time makes the claim checkable, and a marker should be able to hear your answer without playing either track.

Say what the difference does to the music. _The newer version feels heavy and pushed from underneath, and the original sounds lighter._ This is what the second mark is for, and it is the half most people leave off.

zero.answer: “The Amy Winehouse version is heaps better, it has way more soul and the instruments sound amazing.”
zero.why: Three claims and not one of them is about a sound. _Better_ is a preference, _soul_ is a genre word standing in for a description, and _the instruments sound amazing_ names no instrument, offers no colour word and points at no moment in either recording. There is no time anywhere in it, so there is nothing a marker could check. A short answer would be fine here. An empty one is not.

blocks.text: Which version's tone colour suits the song better, and why? Name at least one voice or instrument in your answer.

blocks.summary: Check yourself: five questions on today
items: You counted the beat on both versions. What should the two numbers be, and which element is that? **About 83 beats a minute on the 2006 version and about 108 on the 2007 one, which puts the newer version roughly 29 per cent ahead.** Anything within about five either way means you counted rather than guessed. The element is duration, so it goes into your comparison as a difference in speed and nothing else.

Which version puts more of its sound at the bottom of the range, and where is that easiest to hear? **The 2007 one, and the clearest case is the stretch straight after 0:51, where roughly a fifth to a quarter of everything sounding is in the lowest band.** On the 2006 version that band holds between a hundredth and a twentieth for practically the whole track, which is why it reads as lighter even when it is just as loud.

Where does each version get out of the way, and why does that matter today? **The 2006 version at 2:34, where the level drops to under a third and the floor of the sound nearly vanishes for about ten seconds. The 2007 version never thins out that far: its one sustained drop, at 2:01, only takes it to about three quarters.** It matters because a thinner moment is where a single colour can be heard on its own, so those are the seconds where the naming actually gets done.

One similarity worth writing, in all three parts. **Name it: both versions are the same song underneath, the same melody, the same words and the same chords, each carried by one lead voice with a group behind it. Evidence: the tune you can sing over one is the tune you can sing over the other, and in both of them that tune sits in a single voice rather than being shared around. Effect: because the song itself is held still, everything you can hear that differs is down to the performing, which is how two recordings of one song end up feeling like two different pieces of music to whoever is listening.** The melody, words and chords you can take as given, because that is what makes the 2007 recording a cover. The one-voice-and-a-group half you check the way you check every other name on this page: watch the videos.

The exit question: which version's tone colour suits the song better? **Either version can be defended, and the mark is in three moves rather than in the choice: name a source you actually heard, give it a word from the bank, and say what that word does to the song.** Written out it is one sentence, with the brackets filled from your own listening: _The 2007 version suits it better, because the (source you named) sounds (your word from the bank), and that (what the word does) suits a song that (what the song is doing there)._ Filled in, it looks like this. Say the word you would defend for the lead voice on the 2007 version is _husky_: then your sentence runs _The 2007 version suits it better, because the lead voice is husky, with a grain on it that a smoother voice would not have, and that roughness makes the song sound like somebody telling you something rather than performing it._ That is a full answer if husky is genuinely your word and you can point at the moment that made you choose it. It is worth nothing if you copied it off this page, and a marker can tell, because the next question will ask you where you heard it. Two answers that do not get there at all: _The 2007 one, because it sounds better_, which makes none of the three moves, and _The 2007 one, because it has more low sound in it_, which says where the sound sits rather than what it is like. Register points your ears at the right place. It is not a tone colour, and it will not do the job of one.

weeks.title: Dynamics, Structure and Exam Writing
weeks.intro: This week we finish the toolkit with dynamics, expression and structure, and start writing full responses to the exam question.

lessons.title: Dynamics and expression
lessons.intention: I can identify dynamics and expression and explain their effect.
criteria: I can describe how the volume changes.
I can explain how a change in dynamics changes the mood.

blocks.text: How loud or soft the music is, and the little performance tricks (sliding, plucking, shaking a note) that add feeling.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: A dynamic level is a fact. A dynamic change is an answer.

body.p: Most students write “the music is loud” and stop, which describes one second of a piece and earns nothing. Dynamics is not really about volume. It is about the shape volume makes across time, and what that shape does to you.

body.h: Three things to listen for, in order of what they are worth

ul: **The level.** Loud or soft, right now. Worth naming, worth nothing on its own.
**The change.** Does it grow or fall away, and does it do it suddenly or gradually? This is where the marks start, because you can only hear it by listening across time rather than at one moment.
**The effect.** What that change does to the music and to the listener. This is where the marks actually are.

body.p: **Working rule: if you could answer it by reading one word off the score, it is not analysis yet.** Anyone can see _forte_ written on a page. Only someone listening can tell you whether the music arrived there in one step or crept up on you over ninety seconds, and those two do completely different things to a listener.

body.h: Expression is how a note is played, not how loud it is

body.p: Two players can play the same note, at the same volume, at the same moment, and sound nothing alike. One plays it smooth and joined to the next note, the other cuts it short. One leans on it, the other slides into it from underneath. One shakes the note, the other holds it dead still. That is expression, and it is usually what makes a style instantly recognisable: the same melody played with the articulation of one style and then another stops sounding like the same music at all.

blocks.prompt: We fill these in together. Type the English meaning next to each term.
