blocks.label: Excerpt 1: orchestra
blocks.work: Gustav Holst, “Jupiter, the Bringer of Jollity”, from The Planets, Op. 32
blocks.meta: Recorded 1981 · 7:36 · Berliner Philharmoniker, Herbert von Karajan
blocks.brief: An orchestra has dozens of players and can use any number of them at once. Follow one question the whole way through: how much of the orchestra is playing, and which part of its range?

cues.text: Busy at the top, empty underneath. Something new starts about two and a half times a second, and yet the bottom of the orchestra is silent: the two lowest bands carry under one hundredth of the sound. A texture can be crowded and thin at the same time, which is the first thing this excerpt has to teach you.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/wvfz23jZz6c.json. At 0:04 the sub and bass bands together carry 0.009 of the total energy; the onset detector counts 2.38 events a second over the first eight seconds.

cues.text: The bottom arrives. Nothing above it changed: no new tune, no faster notes. The low register alone goes from under a fiftieth of the sound to nearly a fifth of it, and the whole thing sounds twice as heavy. **Texture can thicken downwards, without a single extra note at the top.**
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/wvfz23jZz6c.json. The bass band rises from 0.013 at 0:10 to 0.177 at 0:16, and overall level roughly triples across the same four seconds (0.090 to 0.341 of peak).

cues.text: The orchestra shrinks to its floor. In four seconds the level falls to about a sixtieth of what it just was, and what is left is almost all low: the top two bands hold under a tenth of the sound between them, against nearly a third a moment before. Very few players, all of them at the bottom.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/wvfz23jZz6c.json. Level falls from 0.516 of peak at 2:35 to 0.008 at 2:40. The high-mid and high bands together fall from 0.316 of total energy at 2:34 to between 0.036 and 0.093 across 2:37 to 2:44, while the bass band holds 0.18 to 0.45.

cues.text: The broad tune, and the most useful thirty seconds in this lesson. The orchestra is nearly as full as it gets, but the notes have almost stopped moving: through here the music starts something new well under once a second, against two to three times a second in the fast music either side. **Full and busy are different things, and only one of them is texture.**
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/wvfz23jZz6c.json. Onset rate falls to 0.38 to 1.25 events a second across 2:56 to 4:08, against 1.5 to 2.5 in the surrounding music, while the six-band spread stays high at 0.78 to 0.84 and the level rises from 0.20 to 0.30 of peak.

cues.text: One of the loudest moments in the movement is one second behind you, and two seconds ahead the level has fallen to under a fiftieth of it. Hold this drop in mind: neither of the other two tracks goes anywhere near this quiet, and that turns out to be the biggest difference between the three.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/wvfz23jZz6c.json. Level 0.508 of peak at 4:36, 0.244 at 4:37, 0.009 at 4:39, and it stays between 0.006 and 0.03 until about 4:57.

cues.text: The fast music returns and the texture rebuilds. Over the whole movement the quiet moments sit about twenty-six times below the loud ones. That number is the one to bring to the comparison.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/wvfz23jZz6c.json. Across the movement the 5th percentile of level is 0.017 of peak and the 95th is 0.446, a ratio of 26.2 to 1.

blocks.note: Nothing above names an instrument, because the measurement cannot name one: it reads register, level and how often something new starts. That is enough to describe a texture, and it is the honest limit of what was checked.

blocks.label: Excerpt 2: EDM
blocks.brief: Nothing here is played by a room full of people. Every layer is switched on or off by one person at a desk, and you can hear the switch. Follow the bottom of the mix, the way you just did with the orchestra.

cues.text: The opening runs for over twenty seconds with no bass at all: the lowest band carries under a hundredth of the sound the whole way. It does not feel empty, because the top is full. Same trick as the orchestra's opening, reached a completely different way.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/_ovdm2yX4MA.json. From 0:04 to 0:22 the sub band holds 0.002 to 0.008 of total energy while the overall level sits steady at 0.25 to 0.32 of peak.

cues.text: The drop. In two seconds the lowest band goes from under a hundredth of the sound to nearly a fifth, and over four seconds the level nearly triples. **This is the same event as 0:14 in the Holst: the floor arriving.** One took an orchestra and one took a fader.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/_ovdm2yX4MA.json. The sub band rises from 0.004 at 0:22 to 0.178 at 0:24 and 0.254 at 0:26; overall level rises from 0.254 to 0.686 of peak across the same four seconds.

cues.text: And off again. In four seconds the bass is removed, and the top carries on untouched. An orchestra cannot do this: its low players cannot stop between one bar and the next and leave everything else exactly as it was.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/_ovdm2yX4MA.json. The sub band falls from 0.139 at 0:38 to 0.004 at 0:42 while overall level only falls from 0.658 to 0.307 of peak, and the high-mid band actually rises.

cues.text: The biggest single moment in the track, and it is an absence. Almost everything stops. The analysis picks this out as the strongest boundary anywhere in the three and a bit minutes, and it is made of nothing being there.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/_ovdm2yX4MA.json. The chroma-novelty peak at 1:20.7 scores 1.00, the highest on the track; level falls to 0.098 of peak, against a track median around 0.35.

cues.text: Listen to the top disappear rather than the bottom. Over four seconds the highest band falls to almost nothing while the low-middle nearly triples: a filter closing over the whole mix. **The layers are all still playing. Only their top halves have been taken away.**
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/_ovdm2yX4MA.json. Between 2:12 and 2:18 the high band falls from 0.153 to 0.004 of total energy while the low-mid band rises from 0.261 to 0.520. Overall level falls by only a third across the same span.

cues.text: The last and loudest drop. Across the whole track the quiet parts sit only about four times below the loud ones, where the orchestra managed twenty-six. Everything here lives in a narrow band of loudness, on purpose.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/_ovdm2yX4MA.json. Across 0:02 to 3:16 the 5th percentile of level is 0.150 of peak and the 95th is 0.652, a ratio of 4.3 to 1.

blocks.label: Excerpt 3: a cappella
blocks.brief: Five singers, no instruments, no samples. Every layer in this texture is a human being who has to breathe. Follow the same question a third time: what is at the bottom, and how many parts are sounding?

cues.text: One voice, and the video's opening silence before it. This is the thinnest any of the three excerpts starts, and it is the only one where you can count the layers by ear from the beginning.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/LRP8d7hhpoQ.json. The track is silent to 0:05; the first sound at 0:06 measures 0.084 of peak, the quietest opening of the three.

cues.text: The bass voice arrives with real bottom on it: the lowest band goes from a two-hundredth of the sound to about a sixth in one second, and the level doubles. Compare that number with 0:23 in the Avicii. It is nearly the same event, and one of them is a person.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/LRP8d7hhpoQ.json. The sub band rises from 0.005 at 0:38 to 0.160 at 0:39 while overall level rises from 0.287 to 0.604 of peak.

cues.text: The bottom vanishes completely and the upper voices are left exposed. This is the strongest boundary in the track, and like the Avicii's it is made of something leaving rather than arriving.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/LRP8d7hhpoQ.json. Chroma-novelty peak at 2:48.1 scores 1.00, the highest on the track. At 2:49 the sub band reads 0.000 and the bass band 0.003, against 0.078 and 0.045 three seconds earlier.

cues.text: The fullest texture of the three excerpts, and the fullest thirty seconds any of them manage. Every voice is in, high in its range, and it stays there.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/LRP8d7hhpoQ.json. Level sits between 0.53 and 0.66 of peak continuously from 3:34 to 4:06, the longest sustained loud stretch measured on any of the three tracks.

cues.text: Now the voices leave from the top down. The middle band falls from a quarter of the sound to under a twentieth of it while the low band takes nearly three-fifths. The opposite of the Holst at 2:36, which shrank to its floor by losing its ceiling all at once.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Texture is the element for this lesson: how many layers are sounding, and where they sit from low to high.
Work through the three excerpts in order using the timestamps. The times are clickable and jump the player.
For each excerpt, write down the two moments where the texture changed most, and say what changed.
Then write your comparison: one similarity and two differences, each with a time and a reason.
Doing this alone? Everything you need is on this page, and the answers are at the bottom.

blocks.text: Compare how texture is used across the three excerpts: one similarity and two differences. Give a timestamp for every point, and say what the difference does to the listener rather than just naming it.

blocks.summary: Check yourself: the comparison, worked
items: **One similarity.** All three build the same way: they add the bottom last. Holst holds the low register out until 0:14, Avicii until 0:23, Pentatonix until 0:39, and in all three the arrival of the bottom is the moment the texture stops sounding light. **Why it works as a similarity:** it is the same musical decision reached by an orchestrator, a producer and five singers, so it says something about texture rather than about style.

**Difference 1: how far the texture can fall.** Across the whole movement, Holst's quiet moments sit about twenty-six times below his loud ones, and you can hear the extreme of it between 4:36 and 4:39. Across whole tracks Avicii's sit about four times below and Pentatonix's about four times below. **What it does:** the orchestra can make you lean in, and the other two never ask you to. Loudness in a modern production is held in a narrow band on purpose, so texture has to do the work that dynamics does in Holst.

**Difference 2: how a layer leaves.** Avicii takes the bass out in four seconds at 0:40 and leaves everything above it untouched, and at 2:12 closes a filter over the whole mix so every layer loses its top half at once. Holst cannot do either: at 2:36 he also takes four seconds, but what is left is a different set of players, not the same players filtered. **What it does:** in the Avicii the change feels done to the music, and in the Holst it feels done by the musicians.

**Another difference, if you want a third.** How busy the surface is. Across whole tracks, something new starts about 3.5 times a second in the Avicii, 2.8 in the Pentatonix and 1.6 in the Holst. **The trap:** that does not make the Holst the thinnest. At 2:59 it is running the fullest orchestra of the movement at well under one event a second. **Full is about how many layers, busy is about how often they move, and they are not the same measurement.**

**The exit question: which style used texture most surprisingly?** Any of the three, if you can point at a time. The strongest answer is Pentatonix at 4:24: a song that spent four minutes stacking five voices ends on one voice, alone, with nearly four-fifths of the sound below 250 Hz. **Surprising because it reverses its own method in the last ten seconds.** An answer with no timestamp is not an answer.

lessons.title: Critical listening: evaluating choices
lessons.intention: I can evaluate interpretive choices in performance.
criteria: I can compare two versions of a work.
I can justify a judgement with musical evidence, against a stated criterion.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Liking a version is not evaluating it - naming the change, and judging it against a stated standard, is.

body.p: Every listening task so far has asked you to analyse: how is this music put together, and what does that do. This one asks you to evaluate, which is harder. You have to commit to a judgement about which of two performances works better, and defend it with nothing but the music.

body.h: The move, and it is only three steps

ul: **Name what changed.** Not “they sound different” - say which measurable thing moved: how often the level steps, how low it sits, how thick the bottom of the sound is, how fast the surface changes.
**Say what that change does.** Not the number again in different words - the effect it has on a listener: it holds tension longer, it sits you somewhere lower, it never lets the level settle.

**Only then, judge it against a stated standard.** More effective _at what_? Building tension, holding contrast, keeping a listener inside one steady mood. Name the standard, then say which recording meets it better, and why.

body.p: **Working rule: name your criterion before you name your verdict, or the verdict is only a preference wearing an argument's clothes.** “I like the Richter better” names nothing that changed, does nothing with it, and answers a question nobody asked. Run all three moves and a marker who disagrees with your verdict still has to give you credit, because the moves are what earn it, not the conclusion.

blocks.label: The evidence
blocks.call: Four measured differences between these two recordings, one measured sameness, and not one of them says which is better.

body.p: Two recordings of the same material, both measured the same way. Four differences came back, plus one surprising sameness, and each one is something you can point at and time, which is what a judgement built on evidence actually needs.

ul: **How often the level moves.** The Vivaldi performance changes its sustained level about eleven times a minute; the Richter, about five and a half. That holds whether you measure the whole Vivaldi recording or only the first three and a half minutes Richter recomposes, so it is a feature of the performance, not of the length.

**How low it sits while it moves.** Across that same span, the Vivaldi's level sits below a fixed quiet threshold for close to half the time measured; the Richter's sits there for under a third. The older performance is quieter for longer and reaches lower; the newer one sits higher and louder throughout.

**Where the sound sits in the range.** Once you leave out the quiet spots, about forty per cent more of the Richter's remaining sound sits below 250 Hz than the Vivaldi's does. More of the Richter's energy is low; more of the Vivaldi's is spread across the middle and top.

**How fast the surface changes, instant to instant.** The Richter's sound changes more between one analysis frame and the next than the Vivaldi's does, on average. More is happening moment to moment in the Richter, even though its level itself moves less often.

**The sameness: tempo.** Vivaldi: about 112 beats a minute. Richter: about 108. Within five beats a minute of each other. Whatever makes these two sound different, it is not speed - so tempo is not a difference to reach for.

body.p: **Working rule: pick one of the four differences above as your evidence, not all four - and pick one the cues below give you a time for.** The first two are cued on both recordings, so they are the ones you can point at. Where the sound sits in the range, and how fast its surface changes, are true of the whole recording rather than of any one second, so use them as context around your evidence rather than as the evidence itself. The fifth item, tempo, is not a difference at all - it is a measured sameness, and knowing that rules out one option rather than handing you one to use. A strong evaluation runs the three-move procedure once, on one measured difference, all the way to a verdict. A weak one lists every number on this page and judges none of them.

blocks.label: Excerpt 1: Vivaldi's Spring, the first movement
blocks.work: Antonio Vivaldi, The Four Seasons: “Spring” (La Primavera), RV 269, movement 1
blocks.brief: This video is the whole three-movement concerto, but Richter's recomposition only rebuilds the first movement, so that is the only span worth comparing. Listen to the first three and a half minutes and stop there; the two movements that follow are not part of this comparison.

cues.text: Tap the beat as it starts. Counted properly, this recording sits at about 112 beats a minute, and when you get to the Richter you will find it within about five beats of that. Hold that number: whatever makes these two performances sound different, it is not going to be speed.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 5, ‘Vivaldi: 112.3 bpm’ and ‘the two performances are within about five beats a minute of each other’ (audio_probe whole-track windows, re-run 25 August 2026).

cues.text: The first big swing. In under a second the level drops to under half of what it just was - a listener who has only just settled into the sound is pulled out from under it without warning.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 7, ‘Sustained steps of x0.42 at 0:39.7’ (audio_measure level events).

cues.text: And climbs back to nearly double, in well under ten seconds. That is the shape of this whole opening: not a fade, a series of steps.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 7, ‘x1.78 at 0:48.1’ (audio_measure level events).

cues.text: Down again, and further this time: to under a third of what it had been a moment before - the second time in under a minute the floor has dropped out from under a listener with no warning at all.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 7, ‘x0.30 at 1:03.7’ (audio_measure level events).

cues.text: And straight back up past double, only four seconds later. That is the fastest reversal in this span, and it is the single moment to point at if you want to argue from one event rather than from the rate: a listener who has just been dropped is hauled back up before they have settled into either.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 7, ‘x2.27 at 1:07.7’ (audio_measure level events).

cues.text: One more step up, one and a half times over - the fifth swing in under fifty seconds, and it is that running unpredictability, not any single swing, that you would argue from.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 7, ‘x1.56 at 1:26.7’ (audio_measure level events).

cues.text: The last, and largest, of the swings picked out for this span: more than double in one step. These six are only the largest named ones, over two minutes; counted properly across the whole first three and a half minutes, this recording steps its level up or down about eleven times a minute, more than twice as often as the Richter does across its own opening. What you have just heard is the shape behind that number, not the whole of it.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 7, ‘x2.14 at 2:03.4’, and point 1, ‘A. Vivaldi, first 3:30 … 11.1’ per minute against ‘B. Richter, whole … 5.5’ per minute (audio_measure level events and level-event count).

blocks.note: Stop the comparison at 3:30. Everything after this point in the video is the concerto's second and third movements, which Richter's recomposition never touches.

blocks.label: Excerpt 2: Richter's ‘Spring 1’
blocks.work: Max Richter, “Spring 1”, from Recomposed: Vivaldi's Four Seasons (2012)
blocks.brief: This recomposes the first movement you just listened to. It runs two and a half minutes against the excerpt's three and a half, so do not listen for the two to line up bar for bar. Listen for how differently each one moves through its own opening.

cues.text: The opening, and this is your zero. Quiet, and it barely moves for the first eight seconds: down slightly, if anything, not up. Hold this level in your ear, because every reading that follows is measured against it. And notice what has already happened by refusing to move: a recording that sits still for eight seconds is declining, from the first bar, to do the thing the Vivaldi does five times in fifty.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 6, rms ‘0.048 at 0:00, 0.047 at 0:04, 0.040 at 0:08’ (audio_probe window 0-40 at 4 s).

cues.text: By here the level has already stepped up by two-thirds in one move, and this exact moment is also the sharpest turn anywhere in the whole track. That is context rather than evidence you can time, so use the level steps when you write.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 6, ‘A sustained step at 0:12.1, x1.67, and the track's highest chroma novelty of 1.00 at 0:11.8’ (audio_probe window 0-40 at 4 s; audio_measure level events and boundary list).

cues.text: Climbing on: roughly twice the level it opened at, and the climb is not done yet, so a listener still gets no moment that feels like arrival.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 6, rms ‘0.106 at 0:20’ against 0.048 at 0:00 (audio_probe window 0-40 at 4 s).

cues.text: Higher again: more than three times the opening level now, and still no arrival - that only comes at the plateau eight seconds later.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 6, rms ‘0.156 at 0:28’ against 0.048 at 0:00 (audio_probe window 0-40 at 4 s).

cues.text: And here the climb stops. The level has barely moved in the last eight seconds: this recording reaches its level in one steady climb over about half a minute, then holds it, rather than stepping up and down the way the Vivaldi does.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L24 point 6, rms ‘0.150 at 0:36’ against 0.156 at 0:28 (audio_probe window 0-40 at 4 s).

blocks.note: Across its whole length this recording changes its sustained level about five and a half times a minute, against the Vivaldi's eleven. That difference is exactly what a steady climb like this one sounds like next to a run of sudden steps like the excerpt above.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Read the three-move procedure for evaluating without just preferring.
Listen to Vivaldi's Spring, first movement, using the cues, and stop at 3:30.
Listen to Richter's ‘Spring 1’ using its cues.
Pick one measured difference from The evidence to use as your own evidence.
Write your evaluation using the three moves, then check it against the worked example.

blocks.text: Evaluate which recording is more effective, using the three-move procedure: name the measured difference you are using as evidence, with a time; say what it does to a listener; then judge it against a criterion you state yourself. Do not write “I like it better” anywhere in your answer.

blocks.question: Evaluate which recording is more effective at creating dramatic contrast.
blocks.lead: This is what an evaluate question is asking for, and this lesson's activity asks the same thing in your own words. Here is one full-mark answer, built from the evidence above and one stated criterion. A different criterion, argued with the same three moves, would earn the same marks.
blocks.model: The Vivaldi recording is more effective at creating dramatic contrast across its opening two minutes. At 1:03 the level drops to under a third of what it had been a moment before, then climbs back past double it four seconds later at 1:07, a swing the Richter never attempts: its own opening does the opposite, climbing in one steady rise over about half a minute and then holding there. Measured across the whole of each recording, the Vivaldi changes its sustained level about eleven times a minute against the Richter's five and a half, so what happens at 1:03 to 1:07 is not an isolated moment but a running feature of the performance. That running unpredictability is what makes it more effective at holding a listener through sudden shifts in level, which is the standard this answer is judging against - a different standard, such as which recording sustains one steady mood for longer, would favour the Richter instead.

rungs.text: Name the recording and the criterion you are judging it against. _The Vivaldi performance, for dramatic contrast._ A verdict with no stated criterion is not yet a judgement, whichever way it goes.

Give the evidence, with a time. _At 1:03 the level falls to under a third, then climbs past double it by 1:07; the Richter's opening manages one gradual climb over about half a minute instead._ A marker should be able to hear it from your words without playing either track.

Say what the evidence does across the whole recording, not just the one moment. _The Vivaldi changes its level about eleven times a minute against the Richter's five and a half, so this swing is a running feature, not a single lucky moment._

State the verdict against the named criterion, and be honest that a different criterion could flip it. _That makes the Vivaldi more effective at holding a listener through sudden shifts in level, though not necessarily at anything else._

zero.answer: “I think the Richter version is better because it feels more emotional and modern.”
zero.why: A preference, not a judgement. It names no measured moment on either recording, states no criterion beyond a feeling, and gives a marker nothing to check against the music. An evaluate question pays for the defence, not for which way the verdict falls, so this earns nothing at all.

blocks.text: What criterion did you judge by, and what timed evidence did you use to defend it?

blocks.summary: Check yourself: four questions on today
items: What are the three moves for evaluating a performance, in order? **Name what changed, then say what that change does, then judge it against a stated standard.** A verdict with no stated standard is a preference, not an evaluation.

Vivaldi's Spring and Richter's ‘Spring 1’ sit within about five beats a minute of each other. So if the two sound different, what can you rule out as the cause? **The tempo.** Whatever the difference is, it is not speed.
How often does each recording change its sustained level? **About eleven times a minute for the Vivaldi against about five and a half for the Richter, so the Vivaldi moves roughly twice as often.**
Why does “I like the Richter better” earn no marks on an evaluate question? **Because it names no measured evidence and no criterion: it states a preference, not a judgement.**

lessons.intention: I can present a clear analysis of a work.

My presentation is clear and well organised.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: A spoken analysis is not a written one read aloud: the excerpt carries the evidence, so your voice only has to carry the effect.

body.p: You have about two or three minutes as a group, and a work has six elements and hundreds of moments where any one of them could be doing something interesting. You cannot say everything, so the actual skill in this lesson is choosing what to leave out, not finding something to say.

body.h: Choosing what to say

ul: Listen through the whole work once as a group and log every moment where an element is clearly doing something, the way you have in every listening lesson this term.

From that list, keep the two or three moments where the element is most audible and most decisive for the piece, not the two or three you personally find easiest to talk about. A subtle change you can defend beats an obvious one you can only describe.
For each moment you keep, decide the shortest excerpt that lets the class hear the change for themselves: a few seconds either side of the boundary, not the whole section leading up to it.

body.p: **Working rule: if you cannot say in one sentence why a moment made your shortlist, it should not be on it.** A moment earns its place because it does something decisive to the piece, not because it is easy to point at.

body.h: What changes when you speak it instead of writing it

body.p: [Lesson 3](/10mus1-2026/sound-detectives/lesson-3/) and [Lesson 9](/10mus1-2026/sound-detectives/lesson-9/) built the four-part response sentence: name the element, say how it is used, say what effect that has, then give your evidence. All four parts still apply here, but the last one changes shape. In writing, your evidence is a timestamp someone else has to go and check. Live, you do not cite the moment, you play it: the excerpt is the evidence, sitting right there in front of the class, which means every word you say afterwards can go straight to the effect instead of describing what people just heard for themselves.

That is also why a viva voce is harder than it sounds. Nobody hands you a script to read from, and the questions that follow a presentation are usually about the moment you chose, not the ones you left out. You need to know why you kept it well enough to defend that choice on the spot, not because you memorised an answer, but because you actually ran the shortlisting steps above.

blocks.call: The rubric marking your Depth Study in November is marking you today, while nothing is riding on it yet.

body.p: The criteria below are not written for this lesson. They are [Step 4, Refine and finalise](/10mus1-2026/depth-study/step-4/) of the Term 4 Depth Study: the same Listening and Investigation rubric that will mark your finished project's presentation in AT4, worth 20 marks and 25% of the course, in Term 4, Week 4. In [Lesson 27](/10mus1-2026/sound-detectives/lesson-27/) you launch that project, and in [Lesson 28](/10mus1-2026/sound-detectives/lesson-28/) you commit to a proposal. You are seeing the rubric before either of those happens.

So today is a rehearsal, not the task. What today marks against this rubric does not go on your report and does not count toward AT4. What it buys you is a look at what a live presentation actually needs to do, against the real band descriptors, while there is still a full term left to fix whatever it reveals.

blocks.summary: Check yourself: presenting live
items: Which one of the four Listening and Investigation criteria is this lesson mainly rehearsing, and how many of the 20 marks is it worth? **Presentation and communication (multimodal or viva voce), worth 5 marks.** The other three criteria are rehearsed elsewhere in this course, not by a live audience today.

What is the difference between playing an excerpt as evidence and playing it as decoration? **Evidence is cued to the exact moment the effect happens and is followed by the spoken effect; decoration is played for atmosphere with nothing specific said about it afterwards.**

What does turning a written response sentence into something you say live actually look like? **Written: 'the texture thins to solo voice at the bridge, which pulls focus onto the words, evidenced by the drop from full band to one voice.' Spoken: play four or five seconds around that drop, then say only the effect out loud, because the audio has already given your evidence.** The four-part shape does not change. Which part carries the evidence does.

Can this page tell you which moments your group should present, or what you should say about them? **No - that depends entirely on the work your group chose, which nobody can know in advance.** This page can hand back the fixed facts: the rubric, the procedure, and the mark allocation. The moments themselves, and what you say about them, are your group's own.

If you were not in the room to hear another group present, how do you run today's real test on yourself? **Play back your own recording, choose one excerpt, and check whether it was cued to the exact moment the effect happens and whether you spoke the effect straight after it or left dead air first.** The test is the same one the lesson teaches; you are just running it on your own work instead of someone else's.
